text.p: The resistance to Indonesian rule in East Timor plans to form a "shadow government", Nobel laureate Jose Ramos Horta was quoted as saying on Friday.
He told Portugal's news agency Lusa during a visit to Macau that up to two thirds of the so-called "shadow government" would be made up of activists in hiding in Indonesia or East Timor.
"We start from the principle that at least half, or two thirds, of these people are to be found in East Timor or Indonesia, and not in exile," he said.
Ramos Horta said that some members of the group had already been selected with the endorsement of Timorese resistance leader Xanana Gusmao, who is in jail in Jakarta.
Ramos Horta, who was jointly awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize with Timor Roman Catholic bishop Carlos Belo, declined to name those who were expected to join the group.

Indonesia invaded the former Portuguese colony of East Timor in 1975 and annexed it a year later. Its occupation is not recognised by the United Nations which considers Portugal to be the administering authority.
